title: How do you answer "What is your biggest achievement?" in a consulting interview?
description: How to answer impact and achievement questions in consulting interviews, with weak and strong example answers that make your role and results clear.
hook: You answer "What is your biggest achievement?" by choosing the result where your personal contribution is clearest, not the most impressive headline, then giving the baseline, what you did, and the measured change. Interviewers want to see that you make things happen and can explain your role precisely. The common mistake is picking something big where your own part is invisible.
body:
What the interviewer is testing

This question is about impact: do things change because you are there? It often doubles as a test of initiative, because the best achievement stories start with something nobody asked you to do. The interviewer is listening for:

  • Your role. What would not have happened without you?
  • A measured result. A before and an after, over a defined period.
  • Why it matters to you. What you are proud of reveals what motivates you.

A weak answer

I was part of the team that launched our company's new app, which now has over a million users.

Why it falls short: impressive, but the speaker's role is invisible. The interviewer will ask "What did you do?" and the story has to start again.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use your own.

I noticed that 40% of people who started our online sign-up gave up at the identity check. Nobody owned the problem, so I pulled the data, interviewed ten people who had dropped out, and found that the photo upload failed on older phones. I worked with an engineer to add a manual alternative and rewrote the instructions. Within a month, completion rose from 60% to 78%. With about 11,000 people starting sign-up each month, that's roughly 2,000 extra customers a month. I'm proud of it because I spotted it, nobody asked me to, and I saw it through.

Why it works: the personal role is unmistakable, the result is quantified and checkable (11,000 × 18 percentage points ≈ 2,000), and it shows initiative as well as impact. The last line tells the interviewer what kind of work energises the speaker.

Separate your contribution from the headline

A large result is not compelling if your role is unclear. Build the answer in four parts: the starting point, the decision you owned, your evidence, and the measured effect. If several teams contributed, say so, then explain exactly where your work fitted.

Be careful with projected results. Here is a hypothetical example. A company receives 250,000 qualified leads a quarter and converts 4% into customers, which is 10,000 customers. You notice one segment gets poor follow-up and propose routing it to a specialist team. A pilot suggests conversion could rise to 5%. At the same volume, that would be 12,500 customers, or 2,500 more a quarter; at an illustrative $300 of first-year revenue each, about $750k a quarter.

That is a strong story, but only if you describe it accurately. Until the full rollout confirms it, say "the pilot suggests about 2,500 more customers a quarter", not "I added $750k a quarter". An honest, measured improvement is more convincing than an inflated company-wide number, and interviewers will probe.

Finish with a trade-off or lesson

A short final line adds depth. Perhaps the specialist team handled fewer leads in total, or the pilot showed that lead quality needed fixing first. Impact is not just a number going up; it is an improvement linked to a goal, with enough evidence to believe you caused it.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing by size. A smaller achievement with a clear personal role beats a famous project you were on the edge of.
  • No baseline. "Completion reached 78%" means little without "from 60%".
  • Claiming projections as results. Say what actually happened and label anything forecast.
  • Only "we". Credit the team, then say "I" for your part.
  • Forgetting why. "Why are you proud of it?" is often the follow-up. Have an answer that says something about you.

Try it now

1. Improve this: "I helped grow the charity's fundraising significantly."

Show the answer

Add the baseline, your action and the result: "Our annual appeal raised $6k. I suggested moving from one big event to monthly online donations, built the page and recruited 40 first donors. The next year we raised $15k." Then add what you are proud of.

2. Your pilot cut processing time from 10 days to 7 for 500 cases a month. How would you state the impact?

Show the answer

"It cut three days off each case, so across 500 cases a month that's 1,500 case-days saved a month in the pilot." If it has not been rolled out further, say so rather than scaling it to the whole organisation.

3. List three achievements and, for each, write one sentence on what would not have happened without you. Which has the clearest answer?

Show the answer

Use the one with the clearest sentence, even if it is the smallest. If none has a clear answer, look for a time you noticed a problem nobody owned and fixed it; those make the best impact stories.

Where to practise next

Next, prepare the weakness question. Your achievement story can double for initiative, so map it in your story bank with the fit interview guide, and use a different story for leadership. For the full list of questions to prepare, see the most common fit questions.
